samples.summary: New `yorkie-service` token is an unscoped, unconditional ALLOW for every document and every method — and the security argument for it ("never leaves the process") is factually false, because the token is transmitted to the Yorkie server by design.
samples.evidence:
`decide()` returns `ALLOW` for any token whose `typ` is `yorkie-service` before any document key, verb or method is examined (yorkie-auth.controller.ts:215-217). The token carries no `sub`, no `aud`, no document scope and no `jti` (yorkie-service-token.ts:42), so a single captured token grants read+write — and `RestoreRevision`/`GetRevision` — on *every* document in the Yorkie project for its whole lifetime (`YORKIE_TOKEN_EXPIRES_IN`, default 10m, operator-tunable upward).

The justification given in the code and design doc is that it "never leaves the process, so nothing outside this server can present one" (yorkie-service-token.ts:24-25; yorkie-auth.controller.ts:212-213; docs/design/yorkie-auth-webhook.md). That premise is refuted by this same file: the webhook only ever sees the token because the *Yorkie server* echoes it back in `body.token` (yorkie-auth.controller.ts:202). `authTokenInjector` exists precisely to hand the token to the SDK, which sends it to the Yorkie server on every RPC (yorkie.service.ts:70-74). So the token leaves the process on every server-side attach.

Attack chain: anyone positioned to observe or hold that transport obtains an omnipotent credential — a Yorkie Cloud / third-party-hosted Yorkie operator, a compromised Yorkie server, or a passive observer when `rpcAddr` is plaintext (`YORKIE_RPC_ADDR` defaults to `http://localhost:8080` and self-hosting docs do not require TLS). They replay it as their own `authTokenInjector` against the same Yorkie project (the project public key ships in every visitor's bundle), the webhook allows unconditionally, and they read and write every workspace's documents. Because the allow ignores the attribute key entirely, the captured token is not even limited to the document the backend was working on.

Hardening: bind the token to something (document key where the SDK permits, a `jti` with a one-shot server-side record, or a distinct secret from `JWT_SECRET` so a captured service token is not also a step toward session forgery), and correct the "never leaves the process" claim so the residual risk is reviewed honestly rather than assumed away.

samples.summary: The deployment's master `JWT_SECRET` is accepted as a command-line argument (`--source-jwt-secret` / `--target-jwt-secret`), exposing it to `/proc/<pid>/cmdline`, `ps`, shell history and CI logs.
samples.evidence: `parseArgs` reads `--source-jwt-secret` and `--target-jwt-secret` straight off `process.argv` (copy-yorkie-documents.ts:83-90), and the usage text advertises them (lines 37-42). On Linux `/proc/<pid>/cmdline` is world-readable by default, so any other local user, sidecar container sharing a PID namespace, or process-listing agent can read the value while the script runs; it is also recorded in shell history and echoed by CI runners that print the command line. The value is not an ancillary credential — it is `JWT_SECRET`, the key that signs session access tokens (`AuthService.accessSecret`, auth.service.ts:58, used by `createTokens` at line 118). Whoever reads it can forge a session for any user id. The pre-existing `--source-api-key` on line 75 has the same shape, but this change adds the highest-value secret in the system to that surface. The function already supports the safe route — `yorkieServiceTokenInjectorFromEnv` defaults to `process.env.JWT_SECRET` (yorkie-service-token.ts:76) — so per-side secrets should come from named env vars (e.g. `SOURCE_JWT_SECRET`) rather than argv.

samples.summary: Silent cross-deployment credential leak: when `--target-jwt-secret` is omitted the target client mints its token with *this* process's `JWT_SECRET`, sending deployment A's all-documents service token to deployment B's Yorkie server.
samples.evidence: Both clients call `yorkieServiceTokenInjectorFromEnv(...)`, which falls back to `process.env.JWT_SECRET` when the per-side option is absent (yorkie-service-token.ts:76). The script's own type comment states the two sides are "different deployments, so they need not share a secret" (lines 14-21), yet the default path signs *both* attaches with the single secret in the running shell. Since the service token is an unconditional ALLOW on every document (yorkie-auth.controller.ts:215), running the copy without `--target-jwt-secret` hands the target Yorkie deployment — a different trust domain, by the script's own description — a live credential minted with the source deployment's `JWT_SECRET`, which its operator can replay against the source's webhook for full read/write on every source document. The fallback is silent: nothing warns that a foreign endpoint is about to receive a token signed with the local secret. It should either require both secrets explicitly when the two rpc addresses differ, or refuse to reuse one secret across two addresses.

samples.summary: Newly added security comments state the opposite of the enforcement default this same change introduces, telling a future reader the deployment is allow-all when it is not (and vice versa).
samples.evidence: This change makes enforcement the default (`isYorkieAuthEnforced` returns true unless the literal `false`, yorkie-auth-enforcement.ts:21). But comments added by this same diff say the reverse: notes/src/view/editor.ts:447 — "the Yorkie auth webhook ships in shadow (allow-all) mode by default and so may not refuse the write either" — and notes/src/store/read-only.ts:63-64 — "the webhook allows everything until a deployment both registers its methods and sets `YORKIE_AUTH_WEBHOOK_ENFORCE=true`". packages/docs/src/store/read-only.ts:40 carries the same now-stale claim. Security-posture comments that contradict the enforced behaviour are how the next reviewer mis-scopes a change: someone reading editor.ts:447 will believe a viewer's write is unrefused on a stock install and may weaken a client-side gate on that basis, or conversely leave `=true` set believing it is required. Impact is on future reasoning rather than on running code, hence minor.

samples.summary: The share token is extended to a new surface as a URL query parameter (`?token=`), where it lands in proxy/server access logs, browser history and Referer headers.
samples.evidence: `SharedNotesLayout` passes the share token to `shareTokenImageUploader(token)` (shared-notes-layout.tsx:74), which posts to `/api/v1/shared/images?token=${encodeURIComponent(token)}` (packages/frontend/src/api/images.ts:57). The share token is a long-lived bearer credential that grants editor-role write access to the document (image-share-upload.controller.ts:129-142) and can also be exchanged for a Yorkie token at `GET /auth/yorkie-token` (auth.controller.ts:89). Credentials in query strings are recorded by every intermediary that logs URLs and persist in browser history, so a log-reading operator or anyone with access to the visitor's history obtains editor access. The pattern is pre-existing (shared-document.tsx:332 already does this for docs), so this change widens rather than creates the exposure; a header or POST-body token would remove it.

samples.summary: Operator-supplied values are string-interpolated into a `mongosh --eval` JavaScript program; safe today only because `JSON.stringify` happens to escape adequately.
samples.evidence: `fetchExistingYorkieKeys` builds a JS program by interpolating `JSON.stringify(projectPublicKey)` and `JSON.stringify(candidateKeys)` into template literals and executes it via `execFileSync('mongosh', ['--quiet', mongoUrl, '--eval', evalScript])` (copy-yorkie-documents.ts:161-184). `candidateKeys` derives from `Document.id` rows read out of Postgres (line 248), i.e. from data, not from the operator. JSON string escaping does block the obvious break-out on a modern JS engine, so I could not construct a working injection — hence low confidence — but building executable code by string concatenation from database contents is the shape of the bug, and a `--file`/parameterised query would remove the class. Out of the diff (pre-existing lines), flagged because this change is the one that re-touches the script.

verdict.reason: Every claimed fact checks out in the repo. yorkie-auth.controller.ts:215-217 returns the shared ALLOW constant (defined line 54) for any token whose typ is 'yorkie-service', short-circuiting before CLIENT_METHODS (220), the fail-closed empty-attributes branch (228), and checkAttribute/hasAccess (236-241) — so document key, verb, and method (including GetRevision/ListRevisions, line 83) are never consulted. The payload is unscoped: yorkie-service-token.ts:29-32 and :42 sign only { typ } — no sub, aud, doc key or jti — with lifetime YORKIE_TOKEN_EXPIRES_IN (default 10m, operator-tunable) per yorkie.service.ts:52-55. The security premise in the comments ("never leaves the process", yorkie-service-token.ts:23-25 and yorkie-auth.controller.ts:212-213) is contradicted by the same flow: yorkieServiceTokenInjector (yorkie-service-token.ts:54-62) is wired as the SDK authTokenInjector (yorkie.service.ts:55, :70-74), which transmits it to the Yorkie server on every attach, and the webhook only sees it because Yorkie echoes it back in body.token (yorkie-auth.controller.ts:202). rpcAddr defaults to plaintext http://localhost:8080 (yorkie.service.ts:40-42), and auth.service.ts:99-106 accepts the service typ from any presenter on the shared accessSecret, so a captured token replays as an unscoped read+write credential for every document in the project. No caller or config guard narrows this branch — it is the first identity check and returns immediately — and it is reached from every server-side attach (withDocument) plus ops scripts (yorkieServiceTokenInjectorFromEnv, lines 75-87). This is an unscoped authorization/credential-exposure weakness squarely in the authorization and secrets lanes, so there is no named ground to refute on.

verdict.reason: Every claimed element is present exactly as described. copy-yorkie-documents.ts:83-90 parses --source-jwt-secret/--target-jwt-secret straight from process.argv (argv sourced at line 225), and the usage text at lines 37-42 advertises them as each side's JWT_SECRET. The values flow into yorkieServiceTokenInjectorFromEnv at lines 232-240, whose parameter already defaults to process.env.JWT_SECRET (yorkie-service-token.ts:75-77), confirming the safe env route exists and is bypassed by the flags. Impact is as claimed: JWT_SECRET is the session access-token signing secret (auth.service.ts:58, used at lines 77/85/97/121) and the verification key (jwt.strategy.ts:24, auth.module.ts:25), so anyone who reads it can forge a session for any user id. Command-line arguments are exposed via world-readable /proc/<pid>/cmdline, ps from any local user or PID-namespace-sharing sidecar, shell history, and CI logs. No guard, redaction, or secret-file alternative exists anywhere in packages/backend/scripts. I rejected not-present (all cited lines match; only the reviewer's absolute path prefix differed from the working-directory root), already-guarded (no guard found), and out-of-scope (secret exposure is explicitly named in the Security lane; the pre-existing --source-api-key and credential-bearing --database-url/--mongo-url set a precedent but do not make this exposure unreal).

verdict.reason: Verified all three legs in-repo. (1) yorkie-service-token.ts:75-87 defaults the signing secret to process.env.JWT_SECRET and only warns when the secret is absent, never when it is reused across sides. (2) copy-yorkie-documents.ts:236-241 constructs the target client with yorkieServiceTokenInjectorFromEnv(options.targetJwtSecret); --target-jwt-secret is optional (parsed at 87-90, not in the required-args check at 112-121), so omitting it signs the *target* attach with this process's JWT_SECRET and transmits it to a foreign rpcAddr that the script's own doc comment (lines 14-21, 40-42) describes as a different deployment. The target client is built with no apiKey, so the token reaches the remote server regardless of webhook registration. (3) yorkie-auth.controller.ts:215-217 returns the unconditional ALLOW (defined line 54) for typ === YORKIE_SERVICE_TOKEN_TYPE before any document/verb check, and auth.service.ts:95-107 verifies it with JWT_SECRET (accessSecret) while explicitly accepting that typ (line 102) — so the leaked token is replayable at the source webhook for read/write on every document. No guard exists: nothing compares sourceRpcAddr/targetRpcAddr or refuses secret reuse; the usage text is documentation, not enforcement. In-lane (secret/sensitive-credential exposure across trust domains) and correctly rated major: real disclosure of a live all-documents credential, bounded only by the 10m default expiry and requiring the target operator as the attacker.
